title: Stargazing With Kids: Dark Sky Places and Tips
description: Stargazing with kids: where to find dark skies, when to go, what you can see without a telescope, free apps, and dark sky parks in the UK, Europe and the US.
h1: Stargazing with kids: dark sky places and tips
intro: On a clear, dark night you can see thousands of stars, planets and even the Milky Way. Stargazing is free, magical and great for teens who love space.

image.alt: A fairy-tale castle lit up at night

cardText: Dark sky places, timing and what to look for.

blocks.title: Scout’s stargazing tip
blocks.text: Let your eyes adjust for about 20 minutes, and use a red torch or your phone’s night mode. White light resets your night vision!
points: Meteor showers are a great first target

sections.html: Dark sky parks and reserves have protected, low-light skies. In the UK, places such as Galloway Forest Park, Northumberland and Exmoor are known for their dark skies. The US has many dark sky parks, including several national parks. Even a country park away from streetlights beats a town garden.

• Constellations like the Plough and Orion.
  • Bright planets, which don’t twinkle like stars.
  • The Milky Way on very dark nights.
  • Meteor showers at certain times of year.
Visit a planetarium or space centre: see space days out and museums and science.

faqs.q: What is a dark sky park?
faqs.a: A place recognised for its exceptionally dark night skies and efforts to limit light pollution, making it ideal for stargazing.
